ukmt-cayley-2026-c1.title: Three equations
ukmt-cayley-2026-c1.body:
Let Cayley, Hamilton and Maclaurin have $c$, $h$, $m$ pounds. Then
$$h+1=3(c-1),\qquad m+1=2(h-1),\qquad c+1=\tfrac14(m-1).$$
From the first, $h=3c-4$. From the third, $m=4c+5$. Substituting both into the second: $4c+6=2(3c-5)=6c-10$, so $c=8$. Then $h=20$ and $m=37$. (Check: $21=3\cdot7$, $38=2\cdot19$, $9=\frac14\cdot36$.)

If Cayley and Hamilton each give Maclaurin 1 pound: Cayley has $7$, Hamilton $19$, together $26$; Maclaurin has $39$. And $39/26=1.5$.

**Answer: $\frac32$ times** ∎

ukmt-cayley-2026-c2.title: Divisibility by 4 and parity
ukmt-cayley-2026-c2.body:
Label the cells
$$\begin{array}{ccc}a&b&c\\ d&\blacksquare&e\\ f&g&h\end{array}$$
The four numbers are $\overline{abc}$, $\overline{fgh}$ (rows) and $\overline{adf}$, $\overline{ceh}$ (columns, read downwards). Their units digits are $c,h,f,h$ and their tens digits are $b,g,d,e$.

A number is a multiple of $4$ iff its last two digits form a multiple of $4$, i.e. the units digit $z$ is even, and the tens digit is even if $z\in\{4,8\}$ and odd if $z\in\{2,6\}$.

So $c,f,h$ are even. There are only four even digits $2,4,6,8$.
- If $h\in\{4,8\}$ then both $g$ and $e$ must be even: five even cells $c,f,h,g,e$, too many. So $h\in\{2,6\}$ ($2$ choices), and $g,e$ are odd.
- If both $c,f\in\{4,8\}$, then $b$ and $d$ must be even too: again five even cells. So one of $c,f$ is the other element of $\{2,6\}$ (the one $h$ does not use). The other of $c,f$ is in $\{4,8\}$ and its tens digit ($b$ if it is $c$, $d$ if it is $f$) must be even: it is the remaining element of $\{4,8\}$.

*Count:* $2$ choices of $h$; $2$ choices of which of $c,f$ holds the other element of $\{2,6\}$; $2$ choices for which of $4,8$ goes in the other one of $c,f$ (the remaining one then goes in its tens cell). That fixes four even cells; the other four cells are odd, and the digits $1,3,5,7$ go there in $4!=24$ ways. The odd tens digits required by the numbers ending in $2$ or $6$ are automatically satisfied, since those tens cells are among these odd cells.

Total $2\cdot2\cdot2\cdot24=192$.

**Answer: 192** ∎

ukmt-cayley-2026-c3.title: Perimeters and Pythagoras
ukmt-cayley-2026-c3.body:
The points $A,F,E,D$ lie on a line in this order, with $AF=z$. The parallelogram has $AE=BC=x$ and the rhombus has $FD=x$, so $AD=AF+FD=z+x$.

- Perimeter of rhombus $BCDF$: $4x$.
- Perimeter of trapezium $ABCD$: $AB+BC+CD+DA=y+x+x+(z+x)=3x+y+z$.
- Perimeter of parallelogram $ABCE$: $2(AB+BC)=2y+2x$.

The conditions give
$$3x+y+z=1.1\cdot4x=4.4x,\qquad 2x+2y=0.9\cdot4x=3.6x .$$
The second gives $y=0.8x$, and then the first gives $z=4.4x-3x-0.8x=0.6x$.

Now in triangle $ABF$ the sides are $AB=y=0.8x$, $AF=z=0.6x$ and $BF=x$ (a side of the rhombus). Since
$$y^2+z^2=0.64x^2+0.36x^2=x^2=BF^2,$$
the converse of Pythagoras' theorem shows $\angle BAF=90^\circ$. As $F$ lies on line $AE$, $\angle BAE=90^\circ$. A parallelogram with a right angle is a rectangle, so $ABCE$ is a rectangle. ∎

ukmt-cayley-2026-c4.title: Angle chase
ukmt-cayley-2026-c4.body:
Let $\angle ACB=\theta$.

- $DA=DC$, so $\angle DAC=\theta$. The exterior angle of triangle $ADC$ at $D$ is $\angle ADB=2\theta$.
- $AB=AD$, so $\angle ABD=\angle ADB=2\theta$.

*Angle $DEF$.* In the isosceles triangle $ADC$ ($DA=DC$), $E$ is the midpoint of the base $AC$, so $DE\perp AC$ and $\angle DEC=90^\circ$. Since $FE\parallel BC$, $\angle AEF=\angle ACB=\theta$ (corresponding angles). The rays $EF$ and $ED$ lie on the same side of $AC$, with $\angle AEF=\theta<90^\circ=\angle AED$, so
$$\angle FED=90^\circ-\theta .$$

*Angle $DFE$.* $AB=2BD$ and $F$ is the midpoint of $AB$, so $BF=\tfrac12AB=BD$. Triangle $BFD$ is isosceles with apex angle $\angle FBD=2\theta$, so $\angle BFD=\angle BDF=\frac{180^\circ-2\theta}2=90^\circ-\theta$. Also $\angle AFE=\angle ABC=2\theta$ (corresponding angles, $FE\parallel BC$). Angles on the line $AB$ at $F$:
$$\angle EFD=180^\circ-\angle AFE-\angle BFD=180^\circ-2\theta-(90^\circ-\theta)=90^\circ-\theta .$$

So $\angle DEF=\angle DFE=90^\circ-\theta$, and triangle $DEF$ is isosceles with $DE=DF$. ∎

ukmt-cayley-2026-c5.title: Look at the six extreme numbers
ukmt-cayley-2026-c5.body:
Suppose such an arrangement exists. The numbers that can be adjacent to $1,2,3,10,11,12$ are:
- $1$: $4,5,6$; $\ 2$: $5,6,7$; $\ 3$: $6,7,8$;
- $10$: $5,6,7$; $\ 11$: $6,7,8$; $\ 12$: $7,8,9$.

All these neighbours lie in $\{4,\dots,9\}$, so no two numbers of $S=\{1,2,3,10,11,12\}$ are adjacent. Six pairwise non-adjacent places among $12$ places round a circle must be alternate places. So the numbers of $S$ occupy alternate places and every number not in $S$ is adjacent to two numbers of $S$.

But $4$ is not in $S$. The numbers that can be adjacent to $4$ are $1,7,8,9$ (differences $3,3,4,5$), and only one of them, $1$, belongs to $S$. So $4$ cannot be adjacent to two members of $S$, a contradiction.

**Answer: No** ∎

ukmt-cayley-2026-c6.title: Parity and divisibility
ukmt-cayley-2026-c6.body:
If $p,q,r$ were all odd, then $p-5$ would be even so the left side would be even, but $pqr$ is odd. So one of the primes is $2$, and, as they are distinct, exactly one.

**$p=2$.** Then $p-5=-3$, so $3\mid pqr$ and one of $q,r$ is $3$.
- $q=3$: $(-3)(-18)(r-26)=2\cdot3\cdot r$ gives $54r-1404=6r$, so $48r=1404$, $r=29.25$. No.
- $r=3$: $(-3)(q-21)(-23)=6q$ gives $69q-1449=6q$, so $63q=1449$, $q=23$, a prime. Solution $(2,23,3)$.

**$q=2$.** Then $q-21=-19$, so $19\mid pqr$ and one of $p,r$ is $19$.
- $p=19$: $14\cdot(-19)(r-26)=38r$ gives $-7(r-26)=r$, so $8r=182$, $r=22.75$. No.
- $r=19$: $(p-5)(-19)(-7)=38p$ gives $133p-665=38p$, so $95p=665$, $p=7$, a prime. Solution $(7,2,19)$.

**$r=2$.** Then $r-26=-24$, so $8$ divides the left side, while $pqr=2pq$ with $p,q$ odd is divisible by $2$ but not by $4$. No solution.

Check: $(2-5)(23-21)(3-26)=(-3)(2)(-23)=138=2\cdot23\cdot3$ and $(7-5)(2-21)(19-26)=2\cdot(-19)(-7)=266=7\cdot2\cdot19$.

**Answer: $(2,23,3)$ and $(7,2,19)$** ∎
